how-to-fix-an-exposed-git-directory.html.text:
← Git Exposure Checker

How to fix a publicly exposed .git directory

If Git Exposure Checker (or any other check) has just told you a site's .git directory is publicly readable, the order below limits damage first and cleans up second -- doing it in the other order leaves a window where the directory is still readable while you're deciding what else to do.

1. Block web access to .git immediately

This is the fastest step and it stops the bleeding regardless of what caused it. Add a server-level rule that refuses any request path containing /.git/ before it reaches your application, and ship it as its own change first: 

# nginx
location ~ /\.git { deny all; return 404; }

# Apache (.htaccess or vhost)
RedirectMatch 404 /\.git

# Caddy
@dotgit path_regexp \.git
respond @dotgit 404

A CDN or reverse proxy in front of the origin needs the same rule, or a request that bypasses it still reaches an unprotected origin.

2. Treat this as a full-history exposure, not a current-code exposure

A working .git directory lets a free tool such as git-dumper or GitTools reconstruct the entire repository, not just the files currently deployed. That includes every commit -- files and secrets that were added and later removed, branches that were merged and deleted, anything squashed away in a rebase. Assume anyone who found the exposure took a full clone before you fixed step 1, and plan the rest of this around that assumption rather than around what the current checkout contains.

3. Rotate every credential the history ever held

Search the full history for anything that looks like a key, password, or token -- not a grep of the current tree, which only shows what's still there: 

git log -p --all | grep -iE "api[_-]?key|secret|password|token"

Rotate each match at the service that issued it (revoke and reissue, don't just change a config value locally). A credential that was ever committed and later deleted from the code is still valid at its issuer until you rotate it there -- removing it from the repository does nothing to a copy someone already has.

4. Fix the deploy step, not just the server rule

The rule in step 1 is a stopgap that depends on staying in every server config forever. Find out how .git ended up inside what gets served -- the common cause is a deploy script that copies or syncs the whole repository checkout (rsync, a Dockerfile COPY ., an FTP push of the working directory) instead of a build output that never contained .git in the first place. Publish a built artifact, an export, or an explicit file list instead, and the exposure class stops being possible rather than merely blocked.

Once the fix ships, re-run the checker to confirm .git/HEAD and .git/config are no longer reachable: Git Exposure Checker.

how-to-tell-a-real-exposed-git-directory.text:
How to tell a real exposed .git directory from a soft-404 false positive

Requesting /.git/HEAD and getting back HTTP 200 is not, on its own, evidence your .git directory is exposed. Plenty of webservers and CDNs answer every unknown path with 200 and a custom "not found" page -- a pattern usually called a soft 404. A checker that only looks at the status code flags every site behind one of those as exposed, whether or not a real .git directory is actually there. The fix is to look at what the body contains, not just the status it arrived with.

What the two response bodies actually look like

PathStatusReal exposure bodySoft-404 body
.git/HEAD 200 (both cases) ref: refs/heads/main\n <html><body>404 Not Found</body></html>
.git/config 200 (both cases) [core]\n repositoryformatversion = 0\n <html><body>404 Not Found</body></html>

Both rows return the same status code. A checker that stops at "was it 200?" cannot distinguish the left case from the right one -- it would call both "exposed." The difference only shows up in the body.

The exact shapes this tool matches

The checker on this site parses each body against the narrow shape a real git file actually has, not a loose "contains the word ref" guess:

  • .git/HEAD matches only ref: refs/heads/<name> (a symbolic ref) or a bare 40-character hex commit id such as da39a3ee5e6b4b0d3255bfef95601890afd80709 (a detached HEAD) -- nothing else.
  • .git/config matches only a body containing a [core] section, the one every real repository's config opens with because git init writes it.

A generic error page -- even one written to look plausible -- essentially never happens to produce either shape by coincidence.

Worked through on both cases

Case 1: a real exposure. Both probes return git-internal content:

.git/HEAD   -> status 200, body: "ref: refs/heads/main"
.git/config -> status 200, body: "[core]\n\trepositoryformatversion = 0\n"

Verdict: 1 danger-level finding -- the .git directory is publicly readable.

Case 2: a soft-404, same status code on both.

.git/HEAD   -> status 200, body: "<html><body>404 Not Found</body></html>"
.git/config -> status 200, body: "<html><body>404 Not Found</body></html>"

Verdict: no finding -- neither body matched real git-internal content, despite both requests returning 200.

A status-only check sees two identical-looking "200 on .git/HEAD" results and has no way to tell these two cases apart. Checking the body is what makes the difference visible.

Check your own site

The git exposure checker runs a small Node CLI against a site you name, then renders a plain-English report from the JSON it prints -- nothing you paste is uploaded anywhere. Free and local.

← Back to the checker

Common questions

What does a real .git/HEAD file actually contain?

One line, almost always ref: refs/heads/main (or another branch name) with a trailing newline. On a detached HEAD it is instead a bare 40-character hex commit id, such as da39a3ee5e6b4b0d3255bfef95601890afd80709. Nothing else a webserver would plausibly serve at that path looks like either shape.

What does a soft-404 false positive look like on the same path?

A server or CDN configured to answer every unknown path with a 200-status custom error page returns the same status code, 200, for .git/HEAD as a genuinely exposed one -- but the body is generic error-page content such as <html><body>404 Not Found</body></html>, not a git ref or a commit id. A status-only check cannot tell these two 200 responses apart and flags both as exposed.

I got a 200 status on .git/HEAD -- is my site exposed?

Not necessarily. Status 200 only means the server answered; it does not mean the body is real git content. Check the body against the two shapes above: ref: refs/heads/<name> or a bare 40-character hex string. If the body is an error page, a redirect target, or anything else, the path is not exposed even though the status code says 200.

index.html.text:
Git Exposure Checker

Sends two real HTTP GET requests to a site you choose -- .git/HEAD and .git/config -- and checks whether the response bodies are real git-internal content, not just whether the status code is 200. A publicly readable .git directory lets anyone reconstruct your entire committed source history, including files and secrets removed in a later commit, using a free tool such as git-dumper or GitTools. Only point it at a system you own or are authorised to test.

See this checker vs. checking the URL by hand -- the two ways a manual look gets it wrong.

1. Run the CLI against your site

Node.js, no dependencies to install:

node check.mjs https://example.com/ --json

Get check.mjs, probe.mjs, and analyze.mjs from the repo — plain Node, nothing to install. It only ever talks to the URL you pass; nothing goes through this site. Pass the site root (a trailing slash matters) unless you specifically want to check a subpath's own .git directory.

2. Paste the JSON output here

Paste the JSON from step 1 and click Check.

Report

Raw probe results

Common questions

What can someone actually do with an exposed .git directory?

A tool such as git-dumper or GitTools can reconstruct the entire repository from the raw files a webserver serves under .git/ -- not just the current checkout, but the full commit history. That includes any file or secret that was ever committed and later removed in a subsequent commit: an API key rotated out of the code, a config file with a database password, an internal comment. A live directory listing of the deployed site would never show any of that, because it was deleted before deploy -- it is only present in the git history the .git directory carries.

Why does this check the response body instead of just the HTTP status code?

Because a bare status check produces false positives on a common pattern: a webserver or CDN configured to answer every unknown path with a 200-status custom error page (a "soft 404"), rather than a real 404. Under a status-only check, that server would incorrectly report .git/HEAD as "exposed" for every site behind it. This tool instead checks that the response body is exactly what a real .git/HEAD file contains (a "ref: refs/heads/..." line, or a bare 40-character commit SHA for a detached HEAD) and that .git/config contains the [core] section every real git config opens with -- content no generic error page would happen to produce.

Why only .git/HEAD and .git/config, and not the rest of the repository?

Those two are small (normally well under 200 bytes each), and matching real git-internal content in either is already conclusive: if HEAD or config is exposed, the rest of the .git directory almost always is too, since a webserver serving one static file under a path normally serves every file under it. Reading further -- the object database, packed refs, the full index -- would start to look like this tool downloading the repository itself rather than checking whether it is exposed, which is a different, higher-liability action this tool deliberately does not take.

Why does this need a CLI instead of just checking a URL I type into the page?

Checking an arbitrary third-party URL from inside a browser tab runs into CORS restrictions the target site's own headers control, and a page that could reach any URL a visitor types would itself be a server-side request forgery risk. A small local CLI with no such restriction, run from your own machine, is the same shape every other tool in this class (curl, git-dumper, GitTools) uses.

Does a clean report mean my site has no exposed secrets?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class -- a publicly readable .git directory at the path you point it at. It does not check other common source-control or backup exposures (a stray .svn directory, a .env file, a database dump left in the webroot), does not crawl the rest of the site, and only checks the one base URL you give it, not every subpath a real deployment might serve from. Treat a clean report as evidence about this one exposure class at this one path, not a full security assessment.

How to tell a real exposed .git directory from a soft-404 false positive -- the actual response bytes for both cases, side by side.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class -- a publicly readable .git directory at the one path you give it. It does not check other source-control or backup exposures, does not crawl the rest of the site, and cannot see a pattern it doesn't check for. A clean report describes what these two requests found, not a guarantee the site has no exposed secrets.

Already found an exposure? How to fix a publicly exposed .git directory covers the order that limits damage first -- block access, assume full-history exposure, rotate what was ever committed, then fix the deploy step itself.

A publicly readable .git directory is one deployed-artifact secret exposure; Dotenv Exposure Checker asks the same question of a site's own .env file -- a different, and often more directly damaging, exposure since a dotenv file holds live credentials rather than git-internal plumbing. Docker Build Secrets Checker asks the same "is a secret about to be shipped" question of a container image's build layers, and .env.example Drift Checker asks whether your example environment file has drifted from the variables your code actually reads (a different question from whether a real .env is exposed). Once the repository itself is not exposed, Security Headers Checker and CORS Misconfiguration Checker cover two response-header evidence classes worth a pass on the same site, and Backup File Exposure Checker asks the same "read what's actually there, name the exact evidence" question of a leftover backup archive or SQL dump instead of git-internal plumbing.

vs-checking-the-url-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to the Git Exposure Checker

Git Exposure Checker vs. checking the URL by hand

Typing https://example.com/.git/HEAD into a browser and reading what comes back is a real, fast way to spot the obvious case: a plain 404 means nothing is there, and a line reading ref: refs/heads/main is unmistakably a real, exposed repository. It is also the method most people reach for first, and it genuinely works for that one shape of response. This page names no product or company being compared against — "checking by hand" is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseChecking the URL by handThis tool
A plain 404, or a login page, at .git/HEADCorrectly reads as "not exposed"Correctly reads as "not exposed"
The obvious case: body reads ref: refs/heads/mainCorrectly reads as "exposed"Correctly reads as "exposed"
A site that answers every unknown path with HTTP 200 and a custom error page (a "soft 404")Sees status 200, easy to misread as exposedReads the body; a generic error page does not match real git content, so it is reported clean
A detached HEAD — a bare 40-character commit hash instead of a ref: lineEasy to see an unfamiliar hex string and move on, missing a real exposureTreats a bare 40-character hex string as real git-internal content, the same as a ref: line
Corroborating with .git/config tooAn extra request most people skip once HEAD looks clean or looks exposedAlways checks both, and reports when only one corroborates the other
Repeatable in CI on every deployManual, point-in-timeCLI returns a real exit code

Two worked examples

False positive. A site answers every unknown path, including .git/HEAD and .git/config, with HTTP 200 and a generic <html><body>404 - Page Not Found</body></html> page — a "soft 404", common on shared hosting and several static-site setups. Reading the status code alone says "exposed"; neither body matches a real .git/HEAD or .git/config file, so this checker correctly reports the site clean.

False negative. A site's .git/HEAD returns HTTP 200 with the body 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904 — a bare 40-character commit hash (a detached HEAD), not the ref: refs/heads/main line most people know to look for, and .git/config happens to 404. A person scanning for the familiar ref: format can see an unrecognised string of hex digits and conclude nothing is there. This checker's classification treats a bare 40-character hex string as real git-internal content on its own, so it still reports the directory exposed.

When to still just look

If you only need a one-off sanity check on a site you already suspect, and you know to read the body rather than the status code, looking is fine — it costs nothing and you are already there. The gap this tool closes is correctness on the two cases above, and repeatability: the same body check, run again on every deploy, with an exit code a CI pipeline can act on.

Common questions

What does typing .git/HEAD into a browser by hand actually show you?

Visiting https://example.com/.git/HEAD directly is a real, fast way to spot the obvious case: a plain 404 or a login page means nothing is there, and a line reading "ref: refs/heads/main" is unmistakably a real, exposed git repository. That single glance genuinely works for that one shape of response.

Where does checking by hand produce a false positive?

On a site configured to answer every unknown path with HTTP 200 and a custom error page -- common on shared hosting, several static-site setups, and single-page apps that route unknown paths back to index.html. A person checking only the status code sees 200 at .git/HEAD and concludes the repository is exposed, when the body is actually a generic "page not found" message that happens to carry a 200 status. This checker reads the response body and requires it to actually match a real .git/HEAD file (a ref line or a bare 40-character commit hash) before reporting a finding, so a soft-404 page is correctly reported clean.

Where does checking by hand produce a false negative?

When the repository's .git/HEAD is a detached HEAD -- a bare 40-character hex commit SHA such as 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904, rather than the familiar "ref: refs/heads/main" line most people know to look for. A person expecting the ref: line can glance at a bare hex string, not recognise it as anything in particular, and move on -- missing a real, exposed .git directory. This checker's classification treats a bare 40-character hex string as real git-internal content on its own, the same as the ref: form, so a detached-HEAD exposure is still reported as a finding.

Why does this matter for CI, not just a one-time check?

A browser check is a point-in-time, manual look at one URL. A deploy pipeline, a new static-site host, or a webserver config change can expose (or stop exposing) a .git directory at any point after the last time someone happened to check. The CLI here returns a real exit code from the same body classification, so it can gate a deploy the same way a linter or test suite does, rather than depending on someone remembering to look again.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks one specific, well-documented exposure class -- a publicly readable .git directory at the one path you give it. A clean report describes what these two requests found, not a guarantee the site has no exposed secrets.
